evidence.title: CEO birthplace and return comovement
evidence.author: Staer, Arsenio; Ucar, Erdem
excerpts: Purpose The purpose of this study is to investigate whether the CEO’s birthplace location matters for stock return comovement.
Findings This paper demonstrates a new comovement effect based on the CEO birthplace.

We find than at the comovement effect mostly comes from the townsman bias channel, suggesting a positive relationship between investors’ preference for holding stocks in firms whose CEOs are from their locations – townsman bias – and the comovement effect.
The effect remains strong after controlling for industry, CEO cultural and behavioral factors, firm fundamentals, CEO changes and characteristics in various fixed effects setups.
Research limitations/implications The primary limitation of this research is the availability of detailed CEO birthplace information from public sources.
We identified CEOs from the ExecuComp database for our sample period and manually collected their birthplace data.
However, the birthplace information is publicly accessible only for a part of the database, with birth state data being more commonly available than specific birthplaces.
This perception of similarity leads to return comovement via correlated trading shocks leading to implications for portfolio diversification and investment decision-making.

evidence.title: Oncorhynchus spp.: Climate Change, Pacific Northwest Tribes, and Salmon
evidence.author: Jonathan M. Hanna
excerpts: Salmon (Oncorhynchus spp.) are iconic to the residents of the Pacific Northwest, and to none more so than the Native Americans of that region.
For centuries, salmon have played a fundamental part in the cultural, social, economic, and spiritual life of Pacific Northwest tribes.

Salmon play such a central role that the right to fish as they always had was at the heart of the treaties by which these tribes ceded millions of acres of tribal land to the federal government in the mid-nineteenth century.
This tribal fishing right has been repeatedly recognized and its scope solidified in a number of important legal decisions.
At the same time, judicial protection of the treaty fishing right does not mean that the right is safe from jeopardy.
The salmon that these tribes fish for have been beset by many problems, including development, pollution, and overfishing.
The latest and perhaps most serious threat to salmon populations and habitat is climate change.

Fortunately, experience with these other threats to salmon health and the considerable efforts already underway to combat them may put the treaty tribes of the Pacific Northwest in a better position to address the looming effects of climate change.
This article first discusses climate change and how its effects will impact salmon.
Then, it turns to the history of the treaty fishing right, including a brief description of how judicial decisions have upheld that right.

Finally this article discusses various legal and policy strategies by which tribes might work to mitigate or adapt to climate change in order to save salmon, preserve their treaty right to fish, and ensure their tribal identity and way of life.
Salmon are anadromous fish they hatch in freshwater and migrate to the ocean to mature before finally returning to their natal stream to spawn.

evidence.title: Zalaphus (Sea Lion) and Oncorhynchus (Salmon/Steelhead): Protected Predator Versus Protected Prey
evidence.author: William W. Kinsey
excerpts: recent years, the California sea lion (Zabphus calif ornianus) population along the western coast of the United States has grown.
This positive trend signifies a success for the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), 16 U.S.C §§ 1361-1421, enacted in 1972 to protect marine mammals.

However, concomitant with the species' greater abundance is its increased predation in the Pacific Northwest of salmon (Oncorhynchus spp.) and steelhead (Oncorhynchus mykiss) protected under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), 16 U.S.C §§ 1531-1544.
This article reviews how federal laws protect sea lions but allow for nonlethal deterrence and even lethal removal to reduce sea lion predation of other vulnerable species.
Two species of sea lions live in the Pacific Ocean along the West Coast of the United States: the California sea lion and the Steller sea lion (Eumetopias jubatus) .
California sea lion males can weigh up to 1 ,000 pounds while females can weigh up to 250 pounds.
The population of California sea lions has increased from only 50,000 at the time of the MMPA's enactment to more than 200,000 today.
Steller sea lion males can weigh over 2,000 pounds, and females weigh approximately 700 pounds.
The Steller sea lion population consists of two stocks, or populations, west and east of Alaska.

The western stock of sea lions (ranging from Alaska to Asia) has declined from more than 100,000 in the late 1970s to approximately 30,000 individuals by 1990, and subsequently to approximately 20,000 by 1998.

In contrast, the eastern population (ranging along the coast of southeastern Alaska and the western United States) in recent years has increased and decreased in different areas but overall remained relatively stable at approximately 20,000.
Sea lions consume marine and estuarine prey along the West Coast of North America, including salmon and steelhead.

evidence.title: Salmon
excerpts: Salmon (; pl.: salmon) are any of several commercially important species of ray-finned fish that can live in either freshwater or saltwater from the genera Salmo and Oncorhynchus of the family Salmonidae, native to tributaries of the North Atlantic (Salmo) and North Pacific (Oncorhynchus) basins.
Salmon is a colloquial or common name used for fish in this group, but is not a scientific name.

Other closely related fish in the same family include trout, char, grayling, whitefish, lenok and taimen, all coldwater fish of the subarctic and cooler temperate regions with some sporadic endorheic populations in Central Asia.

Salmon are typically anadromous: they hatch in the shallow gravel beds of freshwater headstreams and spend their juvenile years in rivers, lakes and freshwater wetlands, migrate to the ocean as adults and live like sea fish, then return to their freshwater birthplace to reproduce.
However, populations of several species are restricted to fresh waters (i.e.
Folklore has it that the fish return to the exact stream where they themselves hatched to spawn, and tracking studies have shown this to be mostly true.
A portion of a returning salmon run may stray and spawn in different freshwater systems; the percent of straying depends on the species of salmon.
Homing behavior has been shown to depend on olfactory memory.
Salmon are important food fish and are intensively farmed in many parts of the world, with Norway being the world's largest producer of farmed salmon, followed by Chile.
They are also highly prized game fish for recreational fishing, by both freshwater and saltwater anglers.
Many species of salmon have since been introduced and naturalized into non-native environments such as the Great Lakes of North America, Patagonia in South America and South Island of New Zealand.

evidence.title: Salmon P. Chase
excerpts: Salmon Portland Chase (January 13, 1808 – May 7, 1873) was an American politician and jurist who served as the sixth chief justice of the United States from 1864 to his death in 1873.
Earlier, he had served as the 25th United States Secretary of the Treasury in the Abraham Lincoln administration from 1861 to 1864, during the American Civil War.
Chase also served as the 23rd Governor of Ohio from 1856 to 1860, and represented Ohio in the United States Senate from 1849 to 1855 and again in 1861.
Chase is therefore one of the few American politicians who have held constitutional office in all three branches of the federal government, in addition to serving in the highest state-level office.
From the 1850s onward, even as Chief Justice, Chase unsuccessfully sought a presidential nomination.
Born in Cornish, New Hampshire, Chase studied law under Attorney General William Wirt before establishing a legal practice in Cincinnati.
He became an anti-slavery activist and frequently defended fugitive slaves in court.
Chase left the Whig Party in 1841 to become the leader of Ohio's Liberty Party.
In 1848, he helped establish the Free Soil Party and recruited former President Martin Van Buren to serve as the party's presidential nominee.
Chase won election to the Senate the following year, and he opposed the Compromise of 1850 and the Kansas–Nebraska Act.
In the aftermath of the Kansas–Nebraska Act, Chase helped establish the Republican Party, which opposed the extension of slavery into the territories.
After leaving the Senate, Chase served as the first Republican governor of Ohio from 1856 to 1860.

evidence.title: Salmon run
excerpts: A salmon run is an annual fish migration event where many salmon species, which are typically hatched in fresh water and live most of their adult life downstream in the ocean, swim back against the stream to the upper reaches of rivers to spawn on the gravel beds of small creeks.
After spawning, most Atlantic salmon and all species of Pacific salmon die, and the salmon life cycle starts over again with the new generation of hatchlings.
Salmon are anadromous, spending their juvenile life in rivers or lakes, and then migrating out to sea where they spend adult lives and gain most of their body mass.
When they reach sexual maturity, the adults return to the upstream rivers to reproduce.
Usually they return with uncanny precision to the natal river where they were born, and even to the very spawning ground of their birth.

It is thought that, when they are in the ocean, they use magnetoreception to locate the general position of their natal river, and once close to the river, that they use their sense of smell to home in on the river entrance and even their natal spawning ground.
There are also landlocked populations of some salmon species that have adapted to spend their entire lives in freshwater like trout.
In Northwest America, salmons are keystone species, which means the ecological impact they have on other wildlife is greater than would be expected in relation to their biomass.
Most salmon species migrate during the autumn (September through November), which coincides with the pre-winter activities of many hibernating animals.
The annual salmon run can be a major feeding event for predators such as grizzly bears and bald eagles, as well as an important window period for sport fishermen.
This has knock-on effects not only for the next generation of salmon, but to every wildlife species living in the riparian zones the salmon reach.
The nutrients can also be washed downstream into estuaries where they accumulate and provide significant support for invertebrates and estuarine-breeding waterbirds.

evidence.title: Chinook salmon
excerpts: The Chinook salmon  (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) is the largest and most valuable species of Pacific salmon.
Other vernacular names for the species include king salmon, quinnat salmon, tsumen, spring salmon, blackmouth, and tyee salmon.
The scientific species name is based on the Russian common name chavycha (чавыча).

Chinook are anadromous fish native to the North Pacific Ocean and the river systems of western North America, ranging from California to Alaska, as well as Asian rivers ranging from northern Japan to the Palyavaam River in Arctic northeast Siberia.
They have been introduced to other parts of the world, including New Zealand and Patagonia.
Introduced Chinook salmon are thriving in Lake Michigan and Michigan's western rivers.
A large Chinook is a prized and sought-after catch for a sporting angler.
The flesh of the salmon is also highly valued for its nutritional content, which includes high levels of important omega-3 fatty acids.
The Chinook salmon has not been assessed for the IUCN Red List.

According to NOAA, the Chinook salmon population along the California coast is declining from factors such as overfishing, loss of freshwater and estuarine habitat, hydropower development, poor ocean conditions, and hatchery practices.
